questiontext:
If \({{CT:0}} + {{CT:1}} i\) is a root of the quartic equation

\[{{CT:2}} = 0,\]

find the remaining roots.

The remaining solutions are:

[[input:ans1]]
[[validation:ans1]]

How to enter: the elements in curly brackets, separated by commas. For example {1,-2}. The empty set: {}.

How to enter: the imaginary unit \(i\) is typed as the letter i (or %i), and multiplication with a star. For example 3-2*i.

Hint: give your answer as a set, e.g. {5, 9, 21+3*i}. Marks are only given for a complete and correct answer.
generalfeedback:
Outline: The polynomial has real coefficients, so the conjugate of the given root is also a root. The product of the two corresponding linear factors is a real quadratic factor; dividing by it leaves a second quadratic, whose roots are the last two roots.
Step 1 — The conjugate root
Write \(p(z)={{CT:2}}\) and \(z_0={{CT:0}}+{{CT:1}}i\). All coefficients of \(p\) are real, so taking complex conjugates in \(p(z_0)=0\) gives \(p(\bar z_0)=\overline{p(z_0)}=0\). Hence \(\bar z_0={{CT:0}}-{{CT:1}}i\) is a root as well.
Step 2 — A quadratic factor
Both \(z-z_0\) and \(z-\bar z_0\) divide \(p(z)\), and so does their product:

\[ (z-z_0)(z-\bar z_0)=z^2-2\operatorname{Re}(z_0)\,z+|z_0|^2=z^2-2\cdot {{CT:0}}\,z+\left({{CT:0}}^2+{{CT:1}}^2\right)={{CT:3}} \]

Step 3 — Division
Dividing \(p(z)\) by \({{CT:3}}\) (long division, the remainder is 0) gives the quotient, and the remaining roots solve \[{{CT:4}}\]That is, \(p(z)=\left({{CT:3}}\right)\left({{CT:5}}\right)\).
Step 4 — The remaining roots
The discriminant of the quotient is \(\left({{CT:6}}\right)^2-4\cdot {{CT:7}}={{CT:8}}\), so its roots are real:

\[ z=\frac{{{CT:9}}\pm\sqrt{{{CT:8}}}}{2} \]

[[if test="{{CT:13}}"]]This is a double root, \(z={{CT:10}}\), and in a set it is written once. [[/if]]The quotient factors as \[{{CT:11}}=0\] Therefore the remaining roots (besides \(z_0\)) are

\[ {{CT:12}} \]
